messages.subject: Clarification of logNormal sampling function
messages.body_plain:
I'm confused about your parameterisation of the log-normal distribution (manual page 163). As I understand it, this will return densities for y (in linear units), and requires inputs of mu (in log units) and sigma.

For example, if I wanted to specify a log-Normal hyperprior on a variance parameter (which can't be less than zero) with a mean of 2 and a standard deviation of 1 log unit, I would write:

y ~ lognormal(log(2),1)

and this would return y in linear (not log) units. I can then plug y into a lower-level sampling of something like:

expected_value ~ normal(0,y)

Is this correct?

I plugged the formula (p. 163) into R to play around with it, and this gives slightly different values for the mean. Specifically, the mean on semilog axes doesn't always sit at the expected value of 2, but seems to depend on the sigma value such that as sigma gets larger the mean gets smaller. This seems to be caused by the (1 / y) term in the equation you use, which when removed causes the function to behave as I expect (with a mean of two no matter the sigma). What's the reason for this term? Can I use the logNormal function as I outlined above?

Thanks

Tom Wallis

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Clarification of logNormal sampling function
messages.body_plain:
On 1/2/13 10:16 AM, Tom Wallis wrote:
> I'm confused about your parameterisation of the log-normal distribution (manual page 163).

For the Stan parameterizations, we just followed the appendix of
Gelman et al.'s "Bayesian Data Analysis" book.

It's similar to the one used on the Wikipedi page, but uses
deviation (sigma) instead of variance (sigma^2) as a parameter:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution

 > As I understand it, this will
> return densities for y (in linear units), and requires inputs of mu (in log units) and sigma.

There's also discussion of how log normals are defined as
an example in section 11.2, changes of variables.

The idea is that y has a lognormal(mu,sigma) distribution
if log(y) has a normal(mu,sigma) distribution.

> For example, if I wanted to specify a log-Normal hyperprior on a variance parameter (which can't be less than zero) with
> a mean of 2 and a standard deviation of 1 log unit, I would write:
>
> y ~ lognormal(log(2),1)
>
> and this would return y in linear (not log) units.

First a point of clarification.  lognormal(log(2),1)
doesn't return anything.  It's just the name of a distribution
in Stan.  What happens when the above statement is executed is
the total log probability gets incremented as follows:

   lp__ += lognormal_log(y,log(2),1);

You can see this in the .cpp file output by stanc.

The language for talking about units here is confusing at
the best of times.

> I can then plug y into a lower-level sampling of something like:
>
> expected_value ~ normal(0,y)

The expected value of normal(0,y) is 0 so I'm not sure what this
notation is supposed to mean.

> Is this correct?
>
> I plugged the formula (p. 163) into R to play around with it, and this gives slightly different values for the mean.
> Specifically, the mean on semilog axes doesn't always sit at the expected value of 2, but seems to depend on the sigma
> value such that as sigma gets larger the mean gets smaller. This seems to be caused by the (1 / y) term in the equation
> you use, which when removed causes the function to behave as I expect (with a mean of two no matter the sigma). What's
> the reason for this term? Can I use the logNormal function as I outlined above?

See the Stan manual about changes of variables or
read the relevant section of any respectable math stats book,
such as DeGroot and Schervish or Larsen and Marx.  Or
on the Wikipedia:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function#Dependent_variables_and_change_of_variables

Also, expectations may not be what you expect because of
the curvature of the log function.  In thinking about this issue,
you want to study Jensen's inequality:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen's_inequality

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Clarification of logNormal sampling function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

The mean of a log-normal distribution is a function of both mu and
sigma; specifically E[y] = exp(mu + 0.5*sigma^2), which is only equal
to exp(mu) when sigma goes to 0:
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution
The 1/y term comes as a result of transforming from the unconstrained
space of log(x) to the nonnegative space of x. If you get rid of it
then you won't have a properly normalized distribution—effectively,
you're sampling from a distribution that's proportional to a
log-normal with a different mu.

If you want to specify the mean directly, you can say something like
mu = log(ymean) - 0.5 * sigma * sigma;
where ymean is the desired mean for y. That approach is much less
likely to lead to trouble than random fiddling with density functions.

Best,
Matt

messages.body_plain:
It would be easier to help you if you sent us
the code for the model you ran.  (And either send
us the data or let us know its size at least.)

You can look at the R-hat values to see if you've
converged.

You can also try initializing all coefficients to 0;
there's an option from both the command line and from
RStan.  Regressions with very many predictors can be
very unstable when initialized with Stan's highly
dispersed values.  If you want to get fancy, initialize
the coeffs to 0 and mu to the mean of the y in the data.
Alternatively, standardize the y (this affects prior
specifications, but shouldn't matter if you have pretty broad
priors).

If you have the fit, you should be able to check it
against your existing data by calculating the model predictions
and looking at their errors versus the observed data.
You'd usually want to do this for all samples and take
the average to do full Bayesian posterior inference.

- Bob

On 1/3/13 5:14 PM, Dan S wrote:

> Can Stan can be used to fit a clustering model with the number of clusters K to be determined?

That depends on the clustering model. What do you have
in mind?  We can do something like LDA or soft K-means
by marginalizing out the discrete parameters.  I'll
add a chapter to the programming manual on how to do that.

If you want to do something more general like a
non-parametric estimation of K, that's a bit harder
(though often still finitely approximable in practice).

 > I was expecting to see a
> way of doing it in Stan, but as the manual says, discrete parameters are "not directly supported by Stan", and I'm not
> sure if this is a showstopper or not (since K is discrete, as are the cluster labels). I sketched a Stan program with a
> line like:
>
>    parameters {
>      ...
>      int<lower=1,upper=N> clusteralloc[N]
>      ...
>    }
>
> but it seems that's not going to compile since parameters must be real-valued.

Right -- Stan doesn't (yet) support discrete parameters.
Even when it does, it'll probably be more efficient to marginalize
them out of the model (and reconstruct them later if necessary).

> So I'd be grateful for any tips about how
> to create a Stan program that can address this kind of problem.

What you'll wind up doing is creating something like this:

   simplex[K] soft_cluster_alloc[N]

which represents a "soft" cluster allocation.

> I imagine that one way is to relax the problem so every datum is a member of every class, having a mixture of weights,
> but with a sparse prior on the weights so they tend to [0,0,0,1,0,0].

Exactly.  But you don't necessarily need a sparse prior.  If the
sparsity is "real" the data should sharpen the assignment.
At the same time, be warned that soft clustering models like LDA
can be very sensitive to their Dirichlet priors.

> I found a message from Bob implying Stan's design isn't suited for discrete parameters
> <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/vVPW6Rub_3Q/fd_tHXpiAwwJ>, so maybe I should be looking elsewhere. But any
> tips gratefully received.

It's not really ideal for discrete parameters, but we're
working on ways to do it.  It's just not at the top of
our priority list (that's making what we have more efficient and
adding an RM-HMC sampler), because we still don't have good examples
where we need discrete parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Clustering / discrete parameters
messages.body_plain:
Are you sure you really want an MCMC approach to clustering?

The problem is the multimodal posteriors -- you'll never actually
be able to do full Bayesian inference because there's no way to
properly explore the posterior.  You can use something like EM,
or better yet, a variational approach, which will be able to handle
hierarchical models and won't collapse to degenerate solutions like
EM will when there's no maximum to the likelihood (consider clusters
with one point in them and variance approaching zero, which leads to an
unbounded likelihood).   For something like LDA, I'd recommend
Matt Hoffman's implementation (Matt's also behind the NUTS sampler for
Stan and much of the Stan code);  you can find it in Vowpal Wabbit:

   http://hunch.net/~vw/

(Which you have to love for having the same BSD license and
an even more old-school home page than Stan!)

Given that Matt's on the list, he might have some more specific
recommendations given that he's worked on problems like yours.

As far as "inferring the value of the discrete parameters" go,
what you'll wind up getting from MCMC with discrete samples is
a distribution over values represented by samples (variational
inference gives you a parametric approximation to this distribution).
In the marginalized version, this distribution can be defined as
a transformed parameter.  Once you have that, you know all you're going to know
about the discrete params.  At this point, you can then either (a) sample to
include some  randomness, or (b) take the maximum.  But usually working with the

clustering that goes over issues with non-identification of
parameters (which introduces what Watanabe calls singularities)
and with the multi-modal posteriors and makes connections to the
geometric notion of clustering.  As soon as I get the models
working, I'll post again -- probably a few days, because I'm
working on some other things at the moment.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan, glad to see you on the list!

The basic idea of using Dirichlet priors with small concentration
parameters is one of the cornerstones of Bayesian nonparametrics. In
particular, if you say
θ ~ Dirichlet(α/K,...,α/K);
and let K get very large, the number of elements of θ that have mass
significantly greater than 0 will be (roughly) Poisson distributed
with a (finite) mean that depends only on α, not on K. So if you then
have a bunch of cluster identities
z_i ~ Discrete(θ)
then you're expressing the prior intuition that you only expect a few
of the K possible clusters to actually be associated with data.

It is certainly possible to fit these kinds of models using Stan and
HMC/NUTS, basically using the kind of setup that Bob describes in his
note on soft k-means or in an earlier blog post
(http://lingpipe-blog.com/2011/04/14/summing-out-topic-assignments-ld/).
However, it may not be as efficient at finding a decent solution as
the sort of collapsed Gibbs sampling algorithms that are more
traditional. The classic reference on Gibbs for Dirichlet process
mixture models is Neal's 2000 paper "Markov Chain Sampling Methods for
Dirichlet Process Mixture Models," which shows how to let K actually
go to infinity without doing infinite computation. You may also find
the Teh et al. paper on hierarchical Dirichlet processes interesting.

Best,
Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Clustering / discrete parameters
messages.body_plain:
since we can't collapse over the countably infinite random measure (e.g. polya urn / CRP) in a black box set-up, the common approach seems to employ a truncated approximation of the distribution - the locations and weights -  (see ibrahim), which actually does have some nice conditional independence properties.  variations on this approach are also successfully used for dependent dirichlet processes (such as the HDP).  i've also thought about such implementation in the so-called beta-bernoulli process (where the non-parametric beta process produces the mixing measure for the bernoulli process).  paisley specifies a truncated approximation for the beta process measure, though he then focuses on variational point estimates, rather than MCMC sampling.

neal writes about the better mixing achieved under a DP by working with the pair of distribution indicator and location value, rather than directly sampling the parameters (e.g. from the polya urn).  we achieve the same efficiency under the truncated sampler with the stick breaking weights and locations.

if i want to perform inference on the "space of partitions", then I have to (re-)sample the cluster indicators, z, from the predictive distribution (marginalizing over the random measure) as a post-processing step.

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to model binary responses of 3 human subjects under a number of conditions using a GLM, with additional upper (lambda) and lower (gamma) asymptotes. There is quite a lot of data (16740 responses) and I would like to test for interactions amongst a number of factors, meaning that the linear model design matrix is quite large (37 columns). This model takes longer than I expected to sample -- still running in parallel on a 2.3 GHz quad core i7 drawing 2000 iterations from each of 4 chains, after 8 or 9 hours. The model file and data are attached.

In general, how will stan's sampling speed scale with the size of the dataset? Are datasets / models this big going to simply require a lot of time to sample? Should I try to reduce the number of coefficients I'm trying to estimate (columns in design matrix) to make this more feasible? Sorry for these newbie questions; I am not a computer scientist.

I've done my best to vectorise the actual model where possible, but if anyone has further suggestions please let me know.

Thanks as always for your support.

Tom

messages.subject_clean: Stan sampling speed with large dataset
messages.body_plain:
The wall time is going to increase with the number of observations but it isn't the dominant factor. Reducing the number of parameters would help with speed, but then you might be estimating a model that you don't like.

One thing you can do as of v1.1.0 is replace

  for (s in 1:S) {
    row(e_beta,s) ~ normal(0,1);
  }

with just

e_beta ~ normal(0,1);

I think we found before with your model that it was somewhat faster to use vectors of arrays rather than a matrix because the leading index of the former can be accessed more efficiently. Is there some way to sum over the levels of ss and use the binomial density rather than a bernoulli (see section 13.3 of the manual; it depends on whether X varies by individual or only by level of ss)?

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Are you running optimized code (O=3)?  Are you running
from R or from the command line, and if so, how is the
memory on the machine doing overall?  It can be a problem
in general if you get close to swapping and a big problem
if you start swapping (memory into and out of files).

I'm afraid the simple answer is yes, bigger models
take longer to sample.  The time that it takes to
calculate a log probability and gradient
for a model with a fixed set of parameters and priors
will be proportional to the data size plus a constant
for the work done for the priors.  Now if the data's
much larger than the set of parameters, the data size
should dominate the calculations.

The issue is with the posterior geometry.  In some
cases, more data can make the problem faster by more
tightly constraining the posterior.  In other problems,
the hierarchical structure can present problems for the
sampler getting stuck in regions of low hierarchical
variance (see the discussion of Neal's funnel in the manual).

The code's pretty tight as you wrote it.  The only suggestions
I have for improving its speed are to:

1.  Further vectorize this operation:

   for (d in 1:D){

     for (s in 1:S){

       beta[s,d] <- mu[d] + e_beta[s,d]*sigma[d]; # "matt trick" beta.
     }
   }

to

   for (d in 1:D)
     beta[s] <- mu + e_beta[s] .* sigma;

The ".*" is componentwise multiplication as in MATLAB.
This may not even be a noticeable speed improvement, but
it simplifies the model.

2.  Reparameterize your gamma prior:

     sigma ~ gamma(1,0.5);

which is equivalently

     sigma ~ exponential(0.5);

in Stan's notation. This won't save you much time if any
because the gamma implementation's clever enough not to
compute the Gamma function for fixed alpha.  This won't
help much, but then you can go to this:

parameters {
   real<lower=exp(0),upper=exp(20)>[D] sigma_raw;
...
transformed parameters {
   real<lower=0,upper=20>[D] sigma;
   for (d in 1:D) sigma[d] <- log(sigma_raw[d]);
...
model {
    sigma_raw ~ uniform(exp(0),exp(20));
...

This probably also won't make much of a difference because sigma
isn't a very long vector.  It might help with the geometry, though.

3.  Convert x and beta to types:

vector[D] x[N];
vector[D] beta[S];

That is make them arrays of vectors. The reason is that it
doesn't require any copying or allocation in the loops to pull
out a vector member of an array.  Calling row(x,n) has to
do two bad things:  access the values of x in non-local order [because
the matrices are stored column major], and create an intermediate
row vector data structure to hold the results.

4.  Switch to a logistic regression from a probit.  The
cumulative density function Phi() is a lot less efficient
than the inverse logit.

5.  Aggregate the data in y and replace the Bernoulli
with a binomial.  There's an example in the manual section
of optimization on this.  It looks possible because it looks like
x has many repeated rows, and we know ss[n] only takes on
three values for the three subjects.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan's approach for hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have a couple of questions regarding Stan's (NUTS/HMC_DA) approach to hierarchical models. This is just to further my understanding of how Stan works.

Question 1.

Consider a simple hierarchical regresson, where i stands for individuals and j for observations belonging to an individual.

y_{ij} = x_{ij} \beta_{i} + e_{ij}, j=1 to n_{i}, i=1 to I,   \beta_{i} is a vector of coefficients for individual i.

\beta_{i} ~ N(\mu, \Lambda), where mu_{i} is the population mean and \Lambda is a variance covariance matrix.

e_{ij} ~ N(0, \sigma^{2}), where \sigma^{2} is a univariate variance parameter.

In Gibbs sampling (or MH sampling within Gibbs in non-conjugate cases) one works from blocks of parameters, { \beta_{i} }, \mu, \Lambda and \sigma^{2}.

Does HMC_DA or NUTS use an underlying blocking scheme based on the conditional independence structure of the DAG  to reject or accept on a given iteration? That is, does it accept or reject the \beta_{i} for each individual separately, or are the entire set of parameters (individual level and population parameters) accepted or rejected in one go? What are the pros and cons of doing it in one go?

Question 2.

How does Stan handle different variable scales. It appears that a different epsilon is being used for each parameter.  How does this modify the HMC algorithms in the NUTS paper by Hoffman and Gelman? Is there some place where this is documented?

Thanks

Asim

On 1/9/13 1:11 PM, Asim wrote:
> Hi
>
> I have a couple of questions regarding Stan's (NUTS/HMC_DA) approach to hierarchical models. This is just to further my
> understanding of how Stan works.
>
> Question 1.
>
> Consider a simple hierarchical regresson, where i stands for individuals and j for observations belonging to an individual.
>
>
> y_{ij} = x_{ij} \beta_{i} + e_{ij}, j=1 to n_{i}, i=1 to I,   \beta_{i} is a vector of coefficients for individual i.
>
> \beta_{i} ~ N(\mu, \Lambda), where mu_{i} is the population mean and \Lambda is a variance covariance matrix.
>
> e_{ij} ~ N(0, \sigma^{2}), where \sigma^{2} is a univariate variance parameter.
>
> In Gibbs sampling (or MH sampling within Gibbs in non-conjugate cases) one works from blocks of parameters, { \beta_{i}
> }, \mu, \Lambda and \sigma^{2}.

There are many ways to implement Gibbs.

You can do it blockwise or variable-at-a-time.  And
there are lots of choices for sampling in non-conjugate
cases -- BUGS and JAGS make slightly different choices,
but in no case do they fall back to random-walk
Metropolis in multiple dimensions (except insofar as
you can think of Gibbs as a Metropolis method with
a 100% accept probabilty).

I believe BUGS/JAGS do a single variable at a time, which is
a block of 1 for most variables and a block of N for
a size N multivariate type (such as a simplex or covariance
matrix).  JAGS adds some extra intelligence for sufficient
statistics for GLMs, I think.

> Does HMC_DA or NUTS use an underlying blocking scheme based on the conditional independence structure of the DAG  to
> reject or accept on a given iteration?

I'm not sure what you mean by HMC_DA.  Basic HMC is well
described in Radford Neal's handbook chapter, available here:

http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookSampleChapters.html

HMC, like Gibbs or Metropolis, can be blocked.  Just hold a
subset of the parameters constant and run the dynamics on the rest.

This can be particularly beneficial for hierarchical models where
you have reasonable conditional independence or where you can
use exact Gibbs updates for some of the parameters.  Neal discusses
examples.

Stan doesn't do any blocking yet.  Also, Stan does NOT assume
an underlying directed acyclic graphical model structure.  All
we need to have is a definition of the (log) posterior probability
density up to a proportion.  We then follow that function's gradient,
not an underlying graph structure.

> That is, does it accept or reject the \beta_{i} for each individual separately,
> or are the entire set of parameters (individual level and population parameters) accepted or rejected in one go? What
> are the pros and cons of doing it in one go?

It's all done in one go in Stan now.  See Radford's paper, which
has a fair bit of discussion.  The issues are mainly with scaling,
rotation, and varying curvature by position:

> Question 2.
>
> How does Stan handle different variable scales. It appears that a different epsilon is being used for each parameter.

Right.  There's a discussion in Neal's handbook about
different ways to formulate it, and we're going with
varying step sizes in Stan.

Having said that, Yuanjun Gao just finished a global
(non-diagonal) mass matrix adaptation that will allow
some curvature, and that's implemented as a mass matrix.
Again, see Neal's paper.

And in a couple months, we hope to have a full Riemann
Manifold HMC implementation, which uses a very different
(position dependent) technique to deal with rotation and scaling
that's more computationally intensive but can be much
faster to converge and mix after convergence.

>   How does this modify the HMC algorithms in the NUTS paper by Hoffman and Gelman? Is there some place where this is
> documented?

There's no place it's all cleanly documented in simple algorithmic
form that would make it easy to reproduce.  And the Gelman and
Hoffman paper don't have detailed specifics of how the adaptation
works.

There's the code, which is the final word on what we're doing at
any given time.

The short story is that we're using Nesterov's dual averaging to
estimate the step sizes based on the samples in the warmup, then
fixing the step sizes for sampling after warmup.  Then it's just
a matter of whether we fit a single step size or one per
dimension.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: tips on improving mixing in a multivariate mixed response model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: tips on improving mixing in a multivariate mixed response model
messages.body_plain:
I write to report back on the mixing properties of a multivariate, mixed outcomes model, which I attach.   The model is applied to classroom observations of teacher performances.   The performances are scored on multiple dimensions of an instrument that measures the efficacy of lesson delivery, producing multivariate observations.   The observations are attached to a nested object structure of teacher, classroom (section), lesson, and segments (or portions) of a lesson and then multiple ratings.   The observations are scored by multiple raters assigned to lessons.   I attach a paper to appear in psychometrika that describes the nature of the model.   The punchline is that I have multiple response types which share nested multivariate random effects.   I desire to make inference on the dependence structure of those random effects; most importantly, among teachers.

The attached diagnostic plots focus on samples from two sets of parameters:  The multivariate teacher random effects (Delta) and variables associated to cutpoints for ordered outcomes (z).   The mixing is relatively poor with 2500 iterations and 1000 burnin.   The model parameters are sampled in a de-scaled fashion.  So there's nothing else I am able to see that I may next do that would produce an improvement.   Mixing is much better in JAGS, though with priors on covariances induced under factor analytic constructions or with employment of inverse wishart priors.  Runtimes are slow and sampling 2500 iterations is about 25% slower than the required JAGS runtime to produce a converged sample of sufficient length.   The attraction to stan in this application is the ability to employ more options for covariance priors since conjugacy is not required for sampling covariance matrices and stan also more readily handles mixed mode data.

I had hoped for a better result because past runs produced lots of messages that proposals were about to be rejected and this one produced none.  You will see that the chains occasionally even get stuck for a bit, before moving.

I'm hoping that "logging" this application may prove useful as part of understanding the performance of future iterations of stan.  Thanks much for your coaching and patience to compose, compile and run the script.

terrance

messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  It's very helpful to see this huge models
and get reports on performance (especially vs. JAGS).
And to get a user perspective.

We really need to do a better job on that warning
message.  The rejections are just for single states
on the Hamiltonian path, not of the whole proposal
(which is slice sampled along the path).  Just think
of this as producing an example way below the slice.
Now if it happens on the first step of the leapfrog algorithm,
you will get a rejection.

Over the next few months, we'll speed up the multivariate
models by at least an order of magnitude.  Right now,
we're doing all the derivatives by brute-force auto-dif,
but we can be more clever about this and do all the computations
and gradients using double values and then propagate.
We'll also vectorize them, but I doubt that's your issue.

But even so, we're not going to be able to speed up things like
your rescaling in the transformed parameters block, which
explicitly calls a cholesky decomposition.  There may be a better
way to factor that in terms of algebraic operations that have
better auto-dif behavior.

Nothing else jumps out at me that's going to be a huge gain,
but I'm guessing all those Cholesky factorizations are a killer.

- Bob

> I write to report back on the mixing properties of a multivariate, mixed outcomes model, which I attach.   The model is
> applied to classroom observations of teacher performances.   The performances are scored on multiple dimensions of an
> instrument that measures the efficacy of lesson delivery, producing multivariate observations.   The observations are
> attached to a nested object structure of teacher, classroom (section), lesson, and segments (or portions) of a lesson
> and then multiple ratings.   The observations are scored by multiple raters assigned to lessons.   I attach a paper to
> appear in psychometrika that describes the nature of the model.   The punchline is that I have multiple response types
> which share nested multivariate random effects.   I desire to make inference on the dependence structure of those random
> effects; most importantly, among teachers.
>
> The attached diagnostic plots focus on samples from two sets of parameters:  The multivariate teacher random effects
> (Delta) and variables associated to cutpoints for ordered outcomes (z).   The mixing is relatively poor with 2500
> iterations and 1000 burnin.   The model parameters are sampled in a de-scaled fashion.  So there's nothing else I am
> able to see that I may next do that would produce an improvement.   Mixing is much better in JAGS, though with priors on
> covariances induced under factor analytic constructions or with employment of inverse wishart priors.  Runtimes are slow
> and sampling 2500 iterations is about 25% slower than the required JAGS runtime to produce a converged sample of
> sufficient length.   The attraction to stan in this application is the ability to employ more options for covariance
> priors since conjugacy is not required for sampling covariance matrices and stan also more readily handles mixed mode data.
>
> I had hoped for a better result because past runs produced lots of messages that proposals were about to be rejected and
> this one produced none.  You will see that the chains occasionally even get stuck for a bit, before moving.
>
> I'm hoping that "logging" this application may prove useful as part of understanding the performance of future
> iterations of stan.  Thanks much for your coaching and patience to compose, compile and run the script.

messages.body_plain:
thanks, Bob.  Too bad i couldn't achieve reasonable mixing - I know you're looking more general formulations for the mass matrix to reduce the scale sensitivity.   I'm curious, what do you mean by "propagate"?  As a non-developer, my mental picture of the auto-diff is that it is conducting repeated numerical differentiations on each of the multiple no u-turn steps that compose a proposal.  If it were possible to use symbolic gradient computations, then one could just compute the structure, once, and the rest reduces to filling a matrix.   Within a numerical approach, i understand you could vectorize the gradient computations for speed; otherwise, isn't it about avoiding duplicate computations?

messages.subject: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.subject_clean: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.body_plain:
Before discussing why what Marcel Jonker wants to do is
equivalent to spike-and-slab priors and why spike-and-slab
priors are inefficient to implement in Stan, let me point
everyone to what Andrew has to say on spike-and-slab priors
for Bayesian inference:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/09/prior-distributions-for-regression-coefficients/

Below is a direct reply with an explanation of what's
needed in Stan.

On 1/6/13 7:12 AM, M.F. Jonker wrote:
...
> I posted a simpler form of this model on the STAN mailing list, but I
 > wasn't sure whether the derivations would significantly change for the more complicated models.
 > The confusing stuff, however, is mostly in the data transformations.

> If you just disregard the data transformations and assume only a single set of
 > political dummies subject to Bayesian variable selection (as you suggested), would that
 > be a solution? See the attached files.

Thanks for the simpler model.  I'll try to generalize
a bit.  The basic idea is to do variable selection for
a regression model by including boolean indicator variables.
Marcel sketched out something that looked like this:

   parameters {
     vector[K] beta_raw;             // values
     int<lower=0,upper=1> ind[K];    // indicators
   ...
   transformed parameters {
     vector[K] beta;                 // value or 0
     for (k in 1:K)
       beta[k] <- ind[k] * beta_raw[k];
   ...
   model {
     for (k in 1:K)  ind[k] ~ ...   // priors
     for (k in 1:K)  beta_raw[k] ~ ...
     for (n in 1:N)  y[n] ~ ... x[n] beta ...

This codes up what is effectively a spike-and-slab prior.

The current version of Stan (1.1.0) does not support
discrete parameters, so this model won't compile.  But even
if it did, this kind of model would be problematic for the
way Stan evaluates models.  The problem is that if ind[k] = 0,
then the term beta_raw only shows up in its prior.  So on any
iteration where ind[k] = 0, the betas would wander off according
to their prior, whereas where ind[k] = 1, they show up in the
regression term through beta.  This would almost certainly lead
to pretty serious convergence issues.

It's certainly possible to sum out the discrete parameter array ind
-- just sum the likelihood terms over the possible values of ind,
weighting each by its probability in the current model.  But there
are 2^K possible values for ind here, so this won't be efficient
other than for very small number of variables K.  It'd look like this:

vector[K] ind;       // local indicator vector
for (n in 1:N) {     // loop over data
   for (i1 in 0:1) {  // loop over values for indictor
     ind[1] = i1;
     for (i2 in 0:1) {
       ind[2] = i2;
       ...
         for (iK in 0:1) {
           ind[K] = iK;
           lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log Pr[ind|...],
                                      LL(beta .* ind));
       ...
     }
   }

log Pr[ind|...] is the log probability of the indicator values and
LL(beta .* ind) is shorthand for the log likelihood evaluated with coefficients
equal to the elementwise product of the raw coefficients beta
and the selection indicator vector ind.  log_sum_exp(a,b)
= log(exp(a) + exp(b)), and doing it this way stabilizes
the arithmetic..

Note that all the data needs to be visited for each possible value
of ind, so the likelihood takes on the order of O(2^K * N) steps.
So for large K, it's going to be very slow.

This approach does not lose the connection to the raw coefficients that
the true selection-based implementation Marcel suggested.  So it
should actually work to sample even if it's slow.

- Bob

What do we think of double exponential priors on coefficients in Stan? You ought to be able to get good geometry by

-- specifying standard normal priors on the relevant parameters
-- transforming those with the normal CDF (approximation)
-- transforming those to double exponential via its quantile function

Of course, that never yields exact zero coefficient values, but the prior mean / median / mode is fairly spiky at zero.

Ben

On Thursday, January 10, 2013 5:27:50 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Over the next few months, we'll speed up the multivariate
> models by at least an order of magnitude.  Right now,
> we're doing all the derivatives by brute-force auto-dif,
> but we can be more clever about this and do all the computations
> and gradients using double values and then propagate.
> We'll also vectorize them, but I doubt that's your issue.
>
> But even so, we're not going to be able to speed up things like
> your rescaling in the transformed parameters block, which
> explicitly calls a cholesky decomposition.  There may be a better
> way to factor that in terms of algebraic operations that have
> better auto-dif behavior.
>
> Nothing else jumps out at me that's going to be a huge gain,
> but I'm guessing all those Cholesky factorizations are a killer.

Adding a Cholesky matrix as a primitive type would help a lot in this situation and be a lot quicker to implement than various derivative tricks and / or covariance matrix classes.

You can make your own Cholesky matrix in the transformed parameters block out of a vector of parameters as long as you remember to

-- restrict the diagonal to be positive
-- remember the log Jacobian determinant when putting a prior on the covariance matrix

There is a section of the manual in the Optimizing Stan Code chapter that combines these two points to get a Wishart prior on the covariance matrix from normal and chi-squared priors on the free elements of the Cholesky matrix

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.body_plain:
I am curious what Andrew thinks.  The double-exponential
(Laplace) prior (aka L1 regularization or lasso) is all the
rage in the machine learning literature for variable selection
(sparsity induction) purposes.  I know that he and Aleks
Jakulin and crew settled on the Cauchy to use as a prior
for regression coefficients in the flat (non-hierarchical) case.

   Gelman, Jakulin, Pittau, Su.  2011.
   A WEAKLY INFORMATIVE DEFAULT PRIOR DISTRIBUTION FOR
   LOGISTIC AND OTHER REGRESSION MODELS.  Annals of Applied
   Stats.

   http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/priors11.pdf

Just to point out to the poor users confused by
all this inverse-CDF sample transformation business,
you can still use a double-exponential prior just
by specifying it in Stan.  It just won't be as
efficient.

- Bob

On 1/11/13 4:45 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Of course, that never yields exact zero coefficient values, but the prior mean / median / mode is fairly spiky at zero.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.body_plain:
I'm happy with all these options (except the spike/slab).  If users want coefs that are exactly zero, I think we should think of that as an add-on.  For example, I could imagine having Stan take parameters whose posteriors are tight near zero, and then setting then to be exactly 0, and then going on from there to run with constraints.  That could be worth doing, but I think it should be an explicit part of the processing, not something that gets done by the prior.
But, yes, I'm happy with priors such as double-exponential or t.
A

> though. It's heavier-tailed than a normal, but it won't give you

messages.body_plain:
i don't know about the sampling geometry of stan, but maybe the best choice (in terms of selection performance) for a scale-mixture approach such that the resulting fat-tailed priors on the regression coefficient are abs. cont. wrt to the lebesgue measure is the horseshoe (carvalho, polson, scott - 2010).  sometimes a researcher arrives at variable selection in the case of p >> n under some prior expectation of sparsity and these may not be handled with the scale mixtures because they place 0 measure on the exclusion of a predictor.  the author of the original note mentioned something about high correlations among the predictors.  i'm thinking about the same problem and wonder if i might employ a factor analytic model on the predictors and then regress the response on the resulting smaller number of factors using the horseshoe prior.  my purpose is not prediction, but inference on the association of predictors to the response, so the factor definitions are meaningful, rather than just a computational device.  this means that i have to perform a 2-step or separate estimations because i'd otherwise be making inference on the unidentified factor labels in a joint estimation of factors and coefficients from regressing the response on the factors in a single step.  i suppose one could use a DP (as a stick-breaking mixture in stan) in lieu of a factor analytic (or ICA) approach.

i guess my point is that some of using stan have p >> n problems on which we would like to employ a variable selection approach, but we will first have to do some pre-processing to summarize the information in the predictors.

ben, is your point that i might be able to speed up the runtimes if i build the cholesky from a vector of parameters, rather than sampling from a matrix on which i perform a cholesky decomposition?

on a point related to modeling, the model i posted does not appear to be effectively estimable under stan b/c the mixing is poor.  so getting the mixing to go is a gate that must be passed through before further addressing speed.  what worries me about the inability to get the samples to mix for this particular model is that it is common for me to have models where the effective number of parameters grows above some rate with sample size (though it is identified and estimable).   it is my non-technical intuition that the current HMC implementation in stan has a non-negligible probability of choking on such models due to the possible increase in scale variation with sample.  it's my sense that most of the effective number of parameters grows at a very low rate with sample size for most models posted on this list.

terrance

On Fri, Jan 11, 2013 at 2:29 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Thursday, January 10, 2013 5:27:50 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Over the next few months, we'll speed up the multivariate
> > models by at least an order of magnitude.  Right now,
> > we're doing all the derivatives by brute-force auto-dif,
> > but we can be more clever about this and do all the computations
> > and gradients using double values and then propagate.
> > We'll also vectorize them, but I doubt that's your issue.
> >
> > But even so, we're not going to be able to speed up things like
> > your rescaling in the transformed parameters block, which
> > explicitly calls a cholesky decomposition.  There may be a better
> > way to factor that in terms of algebraic operations that have
> > better auto-dif behavior.
> >
> > Nothing else jumps out at me that's going to be a huge gain,
> > but I'm guessing all those Cholesky factorizations are a killer.
>
> Adding a Cholesky matrix as a primitive type would help a lot in this situation and be a lot quicker to implement than various derivative tricks and / or covariance matrix classes.
>
> You can make your own Cholesky matrix in the transformed parameters block out of a vector of parameters as long as you remember to
>
> -- restrict the diagonal to be positive
> -- remember the log Jacobian determinant when putting a prior on the covariance matrix
>
> There is a section of the manual in the Optimizing Stan Code chapter that combines these two points to get a Wishart prior on the covariance matrix from normal and chi-squared priors on the free elements of the Cholesky matrix
>
> Ben
>
>  On 1/10/13 5:15 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> > > I write to report back on the mixing properties of a multivariate, mixed outcomes model, which I attach.   The model is
> > > applied to classroom observations of teacher performances.   The performances are scored on multiple dimensions of an
> > > instrument that measures the efficacy of lesson delivery, producing multivariate observations.   The observations are
> > > attached to a nested object structure of teacher, classroom (section), lesson, and segments (or portions) of a lesson
> > > and then multiple ratings.   The observations are scored by multiple raters assigned to lessons.   I attach a paper to
> > > appear in psychometrika that describes the nature of the model.   The punchline is that I have multiple response types
> > > which share nested multivariate random effects.   I desire to make inference on the dependence structure of those random
> > > effects; most importantly, among teachers.
> > >
> > > The attached diagnostic plots focus on samples from two sets of parameters:  The multivariate teacher random effects
> > > (Delta) and variables associated to cutpoints for ordered outcomes (z).   The mixing is relatively poor with 2500
> > > iterations and 1000 burnin.   The model parameters are sampled in a de-scaled fashion.  So there's nothing else I am
> > > able to see that I may next do that would produce an improvement.   Mixing is much better in JAGS, though with priors on
> > > covariances induced under factor analytic constructions or with employment of inverse wishart priors.  Runtimes are slow
> > > and sampling 2500 iterations is about 25% slower than the required JAGS runtime to produce a converged sample of
> > > sufficient length.   The attraction to stan in this application is the ability to employ more options for covariance
> > > priors since conjugacy is not required for sampling covariance matrices and stan also more readily handles mixed mode data.
> > >
> > > I had hoped for a better result because past runs produced lots of messages that proposals were about to be rejected and
> > > this one produced none.  You will see that the chains occasionally even get stuck for a bit, before moving.
> > >
> > > I'm hoping that "logging" this application may prove useful as part of understanding the performance of future
> > > iterations of stan.  Thanks much for your coaching and patience to compose, compile and run the script.
> > >

Ben

On Friday, January 11, 2013 8:32:44 PM UTC-5, tds151 wrote:
> ben, re; geometry, the model has 3 types of parameters:  multivariate random effects, covariance matrices, and ordered cutpoints.    with your coaching, the multivariate random effects and cutpoints were sampled as standard normals and transformed.  the covariance matrices were disaggregated into correlation matrices and scale parameters.  the correlation matrices were sampled as uniform.   then is the problem likely in the correlation matrices?  since i use the cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrices to scale the standard normals for the random effects, do you think that your point about building a cholesky decomposition from a vector of parameters would solve the problem?

It is hard to speculate about. A uniform prior on a correlation matrix is equivalent to a series of independent but symmetric beta priors on the primitives, which are almost normal. I think that building up a L matrix would help the wall time and the RAM consumption but not the mixing. Really what we need is to see which parameters have dissimilar variances and high correlations. The pairs() function is useful for this, but really only up to about 10 parameters at a time.

Ben

Not to belabor, but a quick additional data point.   The run result I recently reported as demonstrating poor mixing sampled the cutpoints (of an ordered response likelihood) using your approach of generating vectors of standard normals to produce dirichlet-distributed simplex vector cumsum'd to an ordered vector.  The chains do move under this alternative and demonstrate a move towards convergence, but slowly with the chains sometimes getting stuck (not moving) for some iterations.  I also ran an alternative which directly specified a simplex cumsum'd to a vector of cutpoints.   That run just concluded and the chains did not move, at all.  it appears that not a single proposal was accepted.  So, pretty clearly, the use of approach for generating cutpoints enumerated in the manual is much better - due to your point about getting as close to a standard normal geometry.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: variable selection / spike-and-slab priors for regression coeffs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob (and others),

Thank you very much for this topic (!) Based on the initial post, summing out the indicator variables seems infeasible for anything except for a small number of indicator variables. Accordingly, in my particular case, the options comprise looking into some of the mentioned priors, forgetting about variable selection altogether, or let BUGS run a substantial amount of time.. At the moment, the latter seems to be very attractive: in contrast to Bob's sketch of the problem, the BUGS models include informative pseudo-priors to ensure that the betas do not wander off too much when the indicator variables are zero. Furthermore, the models compile, all chains converge from dispersed starting points (albeit very slowly), and most importantly, I get sensible results in terms of time spent in different models and in terms of parameter values. I'm aware that the pseudo-priors require some tuning (which I did based on prior runs of several sub-models without variable selection). I'd also imagine that this approach wouldn't work well for strongly correlated variables, whose values change significantly when others are included and excluded from the model specification. But in this particular case, the BUGS models seem to work well. So I guess my question is whether it's all about efficiency (which is why I turned to STAN in the first place, but STAN cannot estimate these models yet) or whether the approach should preferably not be used for publications at all?

All the best,
Marcel

Thanks, Marcel, for posting back to the list.  Here's my response:

Go ahead and post this answer back to the mailing list.
We want to keep the discussions as open as possible.
Even we don't believe Stan's the best solution for
every problem!

What I'd suggest is seeing if the predictive inferences or
fits you care about are affected by the difference between,
say, a Cauchy prior, a Laplace/double-exponential prior, and
a spike-and-slab prior.  If there's no difference in inferences
you care about, then I'd suggest going with the simplest form
of the model.  You can always talk about effects being fit
near zero and thus not affecting inference (Andrew's preferred
approach) instead of their being fully eliminated (the spike-and-slab
or selection approach).

If there is a difference, and you can motivate the spike-and-slab
inferences, there's your answer.  And the paper will be stronger
for the comparison.  (Sorry that outside suggestions always involve
more work rather than less.)

As an aside (it won't help solve your selection problem), you
can encode what you call "pseudopriors" in Stan.  You just
need to make sure they always contribute to the model by always
including their sampling statements, rather than only including
them in one branch of execution.

- Bob

We've put some thought into licensing issues and
are happy with either of the following two arrangements:

1.  You keep the copyright and release it under
     an open license (preferably BSD to match Stan,
     but other open-source licenses would be OK).

     We then redistribute under a contributed directory
     that lists the contributors, contributions and licenses.

     If there's not too much there, we'd make it part of the
     standard source download.  Alternatively, we can make separate
     downloads for contributed packages.

     The only tricky part is accomodating new versions.  We can
     give people commit priveleges to git or just update with
     pull requests.

2.  You contribute it to Stan.  We license it under BSD
     like the rest of Stan and distribute it with Stan.

     For this, we do need at least an e-mail from you
     explicitly making the contribution and transferring copyright
     to the Stan development team.

     The Stan copyright is joint among the Stan developers.
     We will add developers to the list who make substantial
     contributions, but we don't want to be in the situation
     where every contributed patch leads to more people on
     the developer list (not because we want to hog the credit,
     but because we want to keep decision-making easy).

Is one of these two options OK for you to contribute?

Less preferable would be:

3.  We just put a note on the web page (and in the doc) directing
     people to external tools.  I don't like this as much because
     it involves maintaining links, which have an annoying tendency
     to go stale.

- Bob

messages.subject: Feature Suggestion: Auto determine optimal posterior sample size
messages.subject_clean: Feature Suggestion: Auto determine optimal posterior sample size
messages.body_plain:
One of the bigger time sinks with MCMC modeling is that you dont know how many sampling iterations you should run your model for until you try it. Since sampling for a big model is pretty expensive, you dont want to run it longer than you need to. However running it for too short of a time, then manually checking if more iterations are needed, also takes time & effort.

Given that you already compute heuristics, such as effective sample size per parameter, after running multiple chains, it seems that you could use that to automatically tune the number of iterations to run the simulation for. For instance, you could have the user specify a minimum desired sample size (or a similar measure), then run multiple chains for a few hundred iterations, then compute the specified heuristic and see if it matched the user specified criteria. If not, then you could run each chain for a few more iterations (e.g. extend it by X%), then repeat the process. Something like this might also be useful to auto-determine the optimal duration for the burn-in / adaptation phase.

This could be a huge time saver when dealing with large models that take a long time to run.

Thanks,
Ilya

The bigger issue is when dealing with large models that run for many hours, since the sampling often terminates when you are not at the computer, so you can't check the convergence diagnostics and restart sampling if needed (e.g. you are in a meeting, at dinner, asleep, etc.). Also if the sampling is slow, doubling the sample size can be quite expensive, so it makes sense to check for convergence more often (which would in turn require you to be at the computer and available to manually check the convergence).

Not saying this is critical, but it would be a nice enhancement for working with slow/complex models.

-Ilya

If 100 is lightning-fast, I'll go to 1000, etc.  If it's not quite at convergence and it's no longer running in less than a couple seconds, I'll switch to doubling:  2000, 4000, etc.  Somehow that works ok.  Especially since there's no need to recompile the model each time.

Hopefully this question has not been addressed already, but I have not been able to find an answer. I am having trouble writing a stan code that can incorporate variability in a model predictor. The model itself is a fairly straightforward multiple regression with random effects, but one of the predictor variables are estimates with associated variance. So, for predictor x (a vector. length N) I have a second vector, s (length N), with a unique variance for each value of x. I am trying to write code that will redefine a new vector, x_new, at each iteration of the MCMC run by sampling from the distributions defined by x and s, ie: x_new~normal(x,s). In all of my attempts the posterior mean values of x_new drift away from their intended values, x. This makes sense, because I have had to define x_new in the transformed parameter or model blocks. Stan therefore treats x_new as a parameter with an informative prior. But, what I want is for x_new to be treated as data that varies at each iteration, not as parameters to be estimated.

I am fairly sure this should be possible, but maybe not without a random sampler in the transformed parameters block? Can this be done with stan?.

-Devin

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestion.  We've thought about it
before but not come to any conclusions about the
best way to do it.

Ideally, a user would indicate how many effective
samples they needed for which parameters, then
we'd run until we'd collected enough.

We could build an auto-Andrew that just ran for
5 iterations in one chain to make sure everyting works,
then 2*K iterations if the target is K samples, and if
that wasn't enough, ran for 4*K iterations and so on.  Each
run just throws away previous runs so that the adaptation
period increases.  We'd probably want to just take a new
random seed each time, too.

This is workable and would be easy to implement.

But it's not optimal in the case that adpatation and
the parameters converge quickly but you need a lot of
samples.  I think we can wind up doing about four times
as much work as necessary in the worst case.  If
adaptation is fast and you need a lot of samples,
then running adaptation for half the iterations does
about twice as much work as is necessary.  Then, if you
get close to how many you need and start over for a few
more samples, you can wind up doing almost twice as much
work again.   So something more sophisticated would monitor
convergence of adaptation, then calculate autocorrelation
time, then run about as many iterations as needed.

Something like this is already on our to-do list.
And we're always happy to take code contributions if someone
wants to write one of these in R.  (Or for the command line.)

- Bob

Devin,
You have to do a measurement-error model, i.e. a simultaneous equations model.  I have not followed your details, but sometimes these models look like this:

y[i] ~ N (a + b*x[i], sigma_y);
x_obs[i] ~ N (x[i], sigma_x);

And you need an informative prior on sigma_x.  In this case, the data are y and x_obs, and x is an unknown parameter vector.  I don't think this is exactly your model but the basic idea is that you need a separate line in your model for each observation.

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
What Andrew said.  Switching back to Devin's variable names
and writing out in Stan, you need:

   data {
     int<lower=0> N;       // number of cases
     vector[N] x;          // measurment with error
     vector<lower=0>[N];   // measurement deviation
     vector[N] y;          // observed outcomes
     ...
   parameters {
     vector[N] x_new;      // measurement plus noise
   }
   model {
     x_new ~ normal(x,s);

     for (n in 1:N)
        y[n] ~ ... x_new[n] ...  // use measurement plus noise
   }

The "x_new ~ normal(x,s)" is vectorized, and just
a more compact and efficient version of writing:

   for (n in 1:N)
     x_new[n] ~ normal(x[n],s[n]);

Hopefully the sampling for y[n] can be vectorized, too.

Instead of sampling x_new directly, you can explicitly sample
the measurement noise for each point n:

   epsilon ~ normal(0,s);
   x_new <- x + epsilon;

- Bob

On 1/20/13 9:04 PM, Devin Leopold wrote:
> Andrew & Bob - thanks for your quick replies! As far as I can tell I have been doing exactly what you suggested. So at
> least I am not too far off the mark here... But still, after the model converges the distributions of the x_new values
> have diverged from the error distributions that I specified. I would expect the posterior mean of x_new to be very close
> to x_obs after 1000+ iterations, but they diverge, suggesting that they are being fitted to the model (the opposite of
> what I am trying to do by incorporating predictor error!).

Right -- the x_new[n] values are intended be fitted with
the model.  The typical Bayesian approach treats them as missing
data.  Specifically x_new[n] represents the true value for
case n that was measured as x[n] with noise sigmax[n].

For instance, see:

   Richardson and Gilks, 1993.  A Bayesian approach to measurement error...
   http://www.med.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/joseph/courses/epib-675/richardson.pdf

So you have something like:

   x[n] ~ normal(x_new[n],sigmax[n])

giving you the probablity of observation x[n] given true
value x_new[n] and measurement deviation sigmax[n].

Sometimes you can integrate out the effect analytically.

 > x_obs~normal(x_new,sigmax)  //I have tried with and without this line of code.
 > x_new~normal(x_obs,sigmax)

You only want one of these.

If you have both, what you get in Stan is the
following two lines of code generated in C++,
where lp__ is the total log probability accumulator:

   lp__ += normal_log(x_obs,x_new,sigmax);
   lp__ += normal_log(x_new,x_obs,sigmax);

Because the variate and location parameter are interchangeable
for a normal, this is double-adding the same term to the log
probability.  The usual formulation is opposite of the way
I suggested, which is to use:

    x_obs ~ normal(x_new,sigmax);

That is, model distribution of the measured values x_obs
given the true values x_new and measurement errors sigmax.

Sometimes you also see a model of x_new as well, especially
if you have some other predictors to use for it.

- Bob

I do something analogous when running JAGS models : I compute max(Rhat) and/or min(effective sample size) and re-run the already- adapted and burned-in model until (convergence goal(s) (is|are) fulfilled) or a preset threshold on run length has been "achieved". I usually double the run length and the "thin" parameter at each step, since, in the models I use, the main problem is usually autocorrelation.

This is not (can *not* be) fully automatic : different chains for the same mixture models, for example, are fond of getting trapped in separate regions of the sample space, and detecting this algorithmically is *not* easy (whereas the human eye "gets it" pretty easily on a"suitably chosen" graph). Hence the importance of running as many chains as possible with suitably chosen starting values. A careful analysis of failed nitial runs *do* help here, and often leads to model refinement (or rewriting !). Similarly, an extra effort to model, for example, correlation within parameters is useful.

I have to say that JAGS' feature of being able to restart an already adapted model is a boon here (large autocorrelations)... Ditto for parallel sampling on different cores/CPUs/machines through snow (implemented in the R dclone package).

I have to say that my current practice of  stan is limited (notably due to its current inability to sample discrete-valued parameters). So such tricks are probably doable in stan, but I do not (yet) master it.

HTH,

                                                                                                   Emmanuel Charpentier

> model like the one attached would also converge with sufficient iterations.
>

> 1. Why is n_eff so small?

I have two suggestions to help improve n_eff:

1.  Rescale your model so you're not using distributions like:

   >      real<lower=9.9e5> mu; // source brightness

   ...

   > mu ~ gamma(3,3e-9); //could also be uniform(9.9e5,1.1e6);

Adaptation has to figure out the scale, and the extreme numbers
tax the arithmetic and warp the no-U-turn condition so that changes
to mu dominate  (We're testing a modification to the no-U-turn condition
that is sensitive to the varying step sizes --- it's kosher w.r.t.
stationarity the way it is, but we think we can make it more effective.)

The way to do rescale directly in parameter space would be something like:

parameters
    real<lower=.099> mu_raw;
transformed parameters
    mu <- mu_raw * 1e7;
model
    mu_raw ~ gamma(...exercise for the reader...);

[you'll have to look up our gamma parameterization, which
  has a scale or inverse scale and change that]

Also, do you really need to constrain mu other than to make
it positive?

2.  The constraints have to match the support for variables or you
get too much rejection:

 >      real<lower=0> xsource; // x-position of source

 >      xsource ~ uniform(0, 100);

The xsource parameter should be declared with <lower=0,upper=100>.

> 2. Is there a fundamental problem with the model as specified to expect convergence to actual parameter values?  Or is
> it a matter of increasing to a large number of iterations given the specified priors? (The number of sensors, or
> non-degenerate observations of the sufficient statistic, is 9, and the number of parameters to estimate is 3, so I think
> with enough iterations, the chains should convergence)

No, I don't think any of those things are going to be issues.

> 3.  Is there any way to control the adaptation of step-size directly via r-stan?  Perhaps this would allow some of the
> chains to explore the parameter space more globally.

I'm not sure what you mean by this.  There's not a way to
set varying step sizes directly.  A better approach is to
rescale the variables.

> 4.  When using a previously compiled model for a new fit, are any aspects of the previous 'end-state' used for the new
> samples (i.e. is the last sample from the first run used as the first sample of the second run)?

No.  Only the compiled model executable code is re-used.

The reason is that we want adaptation to run longer if you
restart.  We should provide some more flexible restart options,
like being able to restart at the point adaptation last left off.

The reason we were lazy is that we usually apply a doubling
strategy (or even a multiply-by-10 strategy), where the saving
from restarting adaptation isn't that great.  For instance, you'd move
from 2000 to 4000 iterations and you'd get to reuse 1000 warmup
iterations, which may save around 1/4 of the iterations;  on the
other hand, those initial warmup iterations are usually the most
labor intensive ones.

Another potential motivation is that if warmup got stuck for
some reason (it is a randomized algorithm), it might get unstuck.

It's already on our to-do list -- it's related to the
automatic run to a given n_eff feature request that just went
by on the list.

- Bob

> I do something analogous when running JAGS models : I compute max(Rhat) and/or min(effective sample size) and re-run the

Right -- that's what we'd try to automate.

> This is not (can *not* be) fully automatic : different chains for the same mixture models, for example, are fond of
> getting trapped in separate regions of the sample space, and detecting this algorithmically is *not* easy (whereas the
> human eye "gets it" pretty easily on a"suitably chosen" graph). Hence the importance of running as many chains as
> possible with suitably chosen starting values. A careful analysis of failed nitial runs *do* help here, and often leads
> to model refinement (or rewriting !). Similarly, an extra effort to model, for example, correlation within parameters is
> useful.

Non-identified parameters are indeed problematic.
I take your point that it can't be fully automatic
everywhere.  This is one of the reasons we haven't built it.

> I have to say that JAGS' feature of being able to restart an already adapted model is a boon here (large
> autocorrelations)...

OK -- that's a good suggestion.  We should implement that
first anyway before trying the full automation route.

 > Ditto for parallel sampling on different cores/CPUs/machines through snow (implemented in the R
 > dclone package).

Jiqiang added this capability to RStan.  See the getting
started doc.  You an use any parallelization package --- RStan
just puts the results back together.  (It's nice having
an embarassingly parallel problem like this -- the next deeper
parallelization of an individual chain/gradient calc is much harder.)

> I have to say that my current practice of  stan is limited (notably due to its current inability to sample
> discrete-valued parameters). So such tricks are probably doable in stan, but I do not (yet) master it.

For most mixture models, we can marginalize the continuous ones
by summing out the discrete parameters.  This actually leads to much
more efficient sampling.

Where we haven't been able to do this is with spike-and-slab priors
for regression.

- bob

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, January 21, 2013 8:33:11 PM UTC-5, tds151 wrote:
> Ben, Per your guidance in the attached noted, would the geometry / mixing improve to sample a covariance matrix from the parameters of it's cholesky decomposition with the off-diagonals drawn from standard normals and the diagonals from inverse gammas or folded normals, on the one hand, versus decomposing the covariance matrix into a correlation matrix and vector of scales for sampling, on the other hand?

With standard normal off-diagonals and diagonals being the square roots of chi-squared parameters with particular degrees of freedom, we know the implied covariance matrix has a Wishart distribution. If you put inverse gammas or folded normals on the diagonal, then the implied prior is something else, probably without a name. I don't like imposing priors that I don't understand the implications of, but that doesn't stop some people. But as long as the off-diagonals have independent standard normal priors, the geometry is probably pretty good along those dimensions of the parameter space.

The lkj_corr() prior is equivalent to a bunch of independent student t priors on the primitives, which also probably have good geometry, although not quite as good as standard normals. What you do with the priors on the standard deviations is another question, but as long as the priors are independent, I doubt it would run into too much trouble.

At the moment, it is not possible to get a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, except by declaring a cor_matrix as a parameter and taking the Cholesky decomposition of it, which will spend a lot of wall time on the auto-diff. This is sort of a shame because it creates the cor_matrix by multiplying its Cholesky factor by the transpose. You could write Stan code to mimic the C++ that creates a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, but the code is somewhat opaque. In contrast, constructing a Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix is pretty easy in Stan code, and about the only thing to remember is to make the diagonal positive.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 1/22/13 4:26 AM, Ilya Esteban wrote:
> Just out of curiosity -- given that it takes two lines of code to transform the uniform distribution into the Cauchy, is
> there any particular reason why the built-in Cauchy function is implemented differently and is so much slower?

The problem isn't that Stan's Cauchy density is inefficiently
implemented.  It's the geometry, as determined (to second order)
by the Hessian of the log probability of the unconstrained
parameters.  (Any parameters declared with constraints are
automatically transformed to unconstrained parameters so HMC
can operate with unconstrained support;  the details of the
specific transforms are in the manual toward the back.)

By declaring a uniform variable with constraint that it be
between 0 and 1, then transforming it to a Cauchy implies
a different geometry than defining a Cauchy over an unconstrained
parameter.   It's not clear this particular transform will even
help.  Of course, there are then other ways to do the [0,1]
transform including inverse CDFs.

The reason he built-in Cauchy function can't do transforms
automatically is that it has no idea what the user's intent
is for the log probability function!

As we learn more about how the geometry affects sampling and which
numerical issues come up, we will hopefully be able to provide
pre-packaged solutions that aren't as clunky as defining
transforms.

Another thing we could do is perform variable transformations
under the hood.  That's effectively what we're doing for
parameters declared with constraints.  But I'd prefer to keep
things as direct as possible.

- Bob

On Tuesday, January 22, 2013 9:18:33 AM UTC-5, Asim wrote:
>
> Here is another prior on Covariance matrices that you may find useful.
>
> http://www.uow.edu.au/~mwand/wispap.pdf

Thanks. The authors sent the first draft of that paper to us for comments a few months ago and it is even better now. That said, I'm not sure it is especially applicable to Stan. One of the virtues of that distribution is that stuff is conjugate so it is easy to use in a Gibbs sampler. There is nothing wrong with using conjugate priors in Stan if they correspond to your prior beliefs, but they don't yield any computational benefits for a HMC sampler.

The other thing is that the authors claim that the fact that the correlations are all *marginally* uniform for a certain choice of a hyperparameter is a good thing. To me, this is a bad thing because marginally uniform correlations are *jointly* non-uniform in an extreme and implausible way, where the density is concentrated in the corners of the admissible parameter space so that the correlation matrix is almost singular. I much prefer the lkj_corr prior for correlation matrices, which for the default value of its hyperparameter is *jointly* uniform over correlation matrices of a given size (and for what it is worth, implies that the correlations are marginally beta distributed after a shift-and-scale). Then you could put half-t priors (or something else) on the standard deviations and go from there.

Ben

The hyperparameters should be constrained so that the matrix is positive definite in theory, so double check that you implemented the formula right. Due to numerical imprecision, it may come out as indefinite. Do such errors cause the sampler to stop or just to reject the proposal? The latter isn't really a major problem.

I'm not sure about your other error message, but I remember something like this happening before when a transformation failed the respect the constraint on the transformed parameter's support, due to numerical issues.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Ben and Asim, My question on the  direct construction of the cholesky decomposition of a covariance matrix was motivated by the possibility to improve mixing, which is a gate the model must pass through to be usable.  My model has 3 parameter types:  multivariate random effects, ordered cutpoints, correlation matrices and associated scales.   Sampling pre-transformed standard normal versions of the first two does not produce adequate mixing performance, so I've begun to wonder about the covariance matrix, which i employ only through the cholesky.   In particular, since standard normals are the ideal geometry for stan, I keyed on Ben's comment on constructing a covariance matrix under an IW through the cholesky parameters.   I want to avoid the property of the IW where correlations may be dependent on the variances/scales, but yet use a similar construction mechanism (through the cholesky) as with the IW if this approach improves the mixing performance; otherwise, i would use other approaches for constructing covariance matrices.

terrance.

On Tue, Jan 22, 2013 at 7:00 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Tuesday, January 22, 2013 9:18:33 AM UTC-5, Asim wrote:
> >
> > Here is another prior on Covariance matrices that you may find useful.
> >
> > http://www.uow.edu.au/~mwand/wispap.pdf
>
> Thanks. The authors sent the first draft of that paper to us for comments a few months ago and it is even better now. That said, I'm not sure it is especially applicable to Stan. One of the virtues of that distribution is that stuff is conjugate so it is easy to use in a Gibbs sampler. There is nothing wrong with using conjugate priors in Stan if they correspond to your prior beliefs, but they don't yield any computational benefits for a HMC sampler.
>
> The other thing is that the authors claim that the fact that the correlations are all *marginally* uniform for a certain choice of a hyperparameter is a good thing. To me, this is a bad thing because marginally uniform correlations are *jointly* non-uniform in an extreme and implausible way, where the density is concentrated in the corners of the admissible parameter space so that the correlation matrix is almost singular. I much prefer the lkj_corr prior for correlation matrices, which for the default value of its hyperparameter is *jointly* uniform over correlation matrices of a given size (and for what it is worth, implies that the correlations are marginally beta distributed after a shift-and-scale). Then you could put half-t priors (or something else) on the standard deviations and go from there.
>
> Ben

--

> On Tuesday, January 22, 2013 10:47:42 AM UTC-5, Tom Wallis wrote:
>
>     More generally, is there a way to declare a constrained object (such as the covariance matrix K) within the model
>     block?

Guaranteed constraint enforcement is only available
for parameters, and the covariance matrix for a GP needs
to be constructed, not sampled (though its hyperparameters
may need to be fit).

>     I am not interested in the samples of K but in the samples of the hyperparameters nu, lambda and r, so
>     therefore it seems like an unnecessary memory burden to store samples of K.

Right.  You don't want to store samples of K.

>     However, if I just declare K to be an N
>     by N matrix within the model block then I get errors that K is not positive definite. I suppose there's a better way
>     to constrain the hyperparameters so that K is always positive definite but I'm not sure what this is.
>
>
> The hyperparameters should be constrained so that the matrix is positive definite in theory, so double check that you

> implemented the formula right.  ...

What you probably want to do is add what Radford Neal calls
jitter to the covariance function.  Otherwise, if you have two data points
with identical x values, you won't get a positive definite covariance
matrix.

I coded up all the basic GP models in Stan for the next manual.
The models, sample data, and R code to run them through RStan are
available from our source-code repository here:

   https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/#git%2Fsrc%2Fmodels%2Fmisc%2Fgaussian-process

It includes examples of how to generate from the prior, fit
hyperparameters, calculate the predictive distribution analytically,
and run logistic regressions.

And you can read a version of the latest doc (although not
with the usual fonts because it's done on our build machine) here:

   http://d1m1s1b1.stat.columbia.edu:8080/job/Stan%20Manual/ws/doc/

I also added a chapter on measurement error models and meta-analysis,
and a chapter on mixtures/clustering models (soft K-means, naive Bayes,
LDA).

This will all be in the next release, which we hope to push out pretty
soon.

- Bob

Ah, now I see your model.  Indeed, you want to use
jitter if you have identical inputs (or if you want to
fit a noisy regression rather than an exact one even
without identical inputs).

You should declare and define mu as transformed data,
not as a local model variable.  We really need a zero_vector(N)
function to produce an N-vector filled with zeroes, or even
a general vector(x,N) to produce an N-vector filled with x.

The model will go faster if you vectorize operations
like the binomial sampling by precomputing the p vector.
That is, turn this:

   for (n in 1:N) {
     p[n] <- (gamma + (1 - gamma) * inv_logit( f_x[n] ));
     y[n] ~ binomial(n_trials[n], p[n]);
   }

into

   for (n in 1:N) {
     p[n] <- (gamma + (1 - gamma) * inv_logit( f_x[n] ));
   }
   y ~ binomial(n_trials, p);

We need to get busy vectorizing our basic functions so you could
just write

   y ~ binomial(n_trails, gamma + (1 - gamma) * inv_logit(f_x));

Also, your covar function definition can be vectorized:

   for (i in 1:N){
     for (j in 1:N){
       for (d in 1:D){
         in_sum[d] <- ((x[i,d] - x[j,d]) / r[d]) * ((x[i,d] - x[j,d]) / r[d]);
       }
       K[i,j] <- nu * exp(-lambda * sum(in_sum));
     }
   }

Ideally, this would be written without the d loop by converting
to matrices and vectors and writing:

     K[i,j] <- nu * exp(-lambda * dot_self((x[i] - x[j])/r));

- Bob
