> subdiagonals[0.5 * K * (K - 1)];,

You should use (K * (K - 1)) / 2.

That will produce an integer result.

Any operation involving a real produces a real result.

You could use real to integer conversion like floor(),
but it's better just to do the arithmetic with integers if
you know you'll get an integer result.

>     fixing it by assigning the result to an integer-declared variable doesn't work.

Right -- you can't assign a real to an integer in Stan.
Or in Java.  C++ will let you do it, and of course,
R, etc., are very free with their typing and assignments.

> 1. if one wants to compose the L[i,j] as transformed parameters so that one extract the transformed standard normal
> parameters (against which L is applied), will declaring "count" in a transformed data block allow it to be used in a
> transformed parameters block?

Yes, you can use transformed data in the transformed
parameter block.

You can use a variable in a statement any time after
it has been declared.  Variables in dimension declarations
have to be data.

- Bob

messages.subject: bug in comparison operator code generation
messages.subject_clean: bug in comparison operator code generation
messages.body_plain:
In release 1.1.0, the comparison operators are compiled
to the wrong targets.  Specifically, > is compiled to >=
and vice-versa and < to <= and vice-versa.

I just pushed a patch to the trunk on git.

This motivate us to get the next version out ASAP.

Until then, there's not really a good workaround.

(This one's all my fault -- I had to rearrange the
order to deal with Boost Spirit's greedy parsing
strategy, but I forgot to take the semantic actions
along with the operator literals.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] compile error [assert failure in Eigen]
messages.body_plain:
Jiqiang/Ben/anyone? -- is there some way to
to trap an assertion failure from R?  I didn't
really think it was possible at all for assert
in C++.

To elaborate a bit more, what's going on is
that the Eigen C++ matrix lib is calling operator(),
which is what Eigen uses to extract an element from a
matrix or vector based on its row and column index.

(R)Stan users shouldn't be seeing this error.  We should
be checking all of our matrix dimensions in all
of our matrix functions.  I thought I'd added
checks to the remaining ones, but apparently not.

So what we need to do is figure out which function
is failing to check its inputs.  The print() statements are
helpful here because they can print out how far
you got (though through R there may be buffering
going on).

Daniel and I can track this down and fix it for
the next release.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob,
Thanks for your detailed explanation and helpful comments.

I modified the scaling and support for parameters as you suggested below (stan file attached) and still get an n_eff=2.  I ran the model with a data matrix of size 9 (J) x 100 (N) using a small chain and then a larger one:

fit1<-stan(file='stanmodel_vecpois_SuffStat',data=rad_dat,iter=100,chains=4)

fit1a<-stan(fit=fit1,data=rad_dat,iter=10000, chains=4)

When examining the extracted values, it does seem that chain #2 is pinned to the lower bound of zero for parameters xsource and ysource, and has the most erroneous posterior mean compared to the true parameter values.  Is it this single chain that is reducing n_eff?

Thanks,

Akhil

On Monday, January 21, 2013 12:49:49 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 1/21/13 1:47 PM, akhil wrote:
>
> > I've copied R and stan code below that tries to estimate the location and intensity of a Poisson "source" using count
> > data observed by "sensors."  Each of the sensors is an unknown distance from the source (in Euclidean space), and the
> > Poisson rate at each sensor is related to the (unknown) Poisson rate of the source by an inverse square law in relative
> > distance.  I will attempt to post the data as a R workspace separately, which hold the actual source rate and position
> > in dat$source.rate and dat$source.pos (x,y coordinates), and the observed counts in dat$counts
> >
> > NUTS can get some of the chains to move towards the actual values for source rate and position, but not others (even
> > after several iterations).
>
> Are they pinned against the constraints (lower = 9.9e5 for mu)?
> If so, you need to fix this problem.
>
> > Also n_eff is rather small even for 1000 iterations.  Since NUTS does a great job at
> > estimating a poisson rate for a toy-model (e.g. estimating rate from rpois samples), I thought a slightly more complex
> > model like the one attached would also converge with sufficient iterations.
> >
> > 1. Why is n_eff so small?
>
> I have two suggestions to help improve n_eff:
>
> 1.  Rescale your model so you're not using distributions like:
>
>    >      real<lower=9.9e5> mu; // source brightness
>    ...
>    > mu ~ gamma(3,3e-9); //could also be uniform(9.9e5,1.1e6);
>
> Adaptation has to figure out the scale, and the extreme numbers
> tax the arithmetic and warp the no-U-turn condition so that changes
> to mu dominate  (We're testing a modification to the no-U-turn condition
> that is sensitive to the varying step sizes --- it's kosher w.r.t.
> stationarity the way it is, but we think we can make it more effective.)
>
> The way to do rescale directly in parameter space would be something like:
>
> parameters
>     real<lower=.099> mu_raw;
> transformed parameters
>     mu <- mu_raw * 1e7;
> model
>     mu_raw ~ gamma(...exercise for the reader...);
>
> [you'll have to look up our gamma parameterization, which
>   has a scale or inverse scale and change that]
>
> Also, do you really need to constrain mu other than to make
> it positive?
>
> 2.  The constraints have to match the support for variables or you
> get too much rejection:
>
>  >      real<lower=0> xsource; // x-position of source
>
>  >      xsource ~ uniform(0, 100);
>
> The xsource parameter should be declared with <lower=0,upper=100>.
>
> > 2. Is there a fundamental problem with the model as specified to expect convergence to actual parameter values?  Or is
> > it a matter of increasing to a large number of iterations given the specified priors? (The number of sensors, or
> > non-degenerate observations of the sufficient statistic, is 9, and the number of parameters to estimate is 3, so I think
> > with enough iterations, the chains should convergence)
>
> No, I don't think any of those things are going to be issues.
>
> > 3.  Is there any way to control the adaptation of step-size directly via r-stan?  Perhaps this would allow some of the
> > chains to explore the parameter space more globally.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by this.  There's not a way to
> set varying step sizes directly.  A better approach is to
> rescale the variables.
>
> > 4.  When using a previously compiled model for a new fit, are any aspects of the previous 'end-state' used for the new
> > samples (i.e. is the last sample from the first run used as the first sample of the second run)?
>
> No.  Only the compiled model executable code is re-used.
>
> The reason is that we want adaptation to run longer if you
> restart.  We should provide some more flexible restart options,
> like being able to restart at the point adaptation last left off.
>
> The reason we were lazy is that we usually apply a doubling
> strategy (or even a multiply-by-10 strategy), where the saving
> from restarting adaptation isn't that great.  For instance, you'd move
> from 2000 to 4000 iterations and you'd get to reuse 1000 warmup
> iterations, which may save around 1/4 of the iterations;  on the
> other hand, those initial warmup iterations are usually the most
> labor intensive ones.
>
> Another potential motivation is that if warmup got stuck for
> some reason (it is a randomized algorithm), it might get unstuck.
>
> It's already on our to-do list -- it's related to the
> automatic run to a given n_eff feature request that just went
> by on the list.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
This is a neat model.

Yes, a single chain getting stuck will lower n_eff for
the collection, because we're using a cross-chain estimator
of variance in our n_eff calculations (see the manual).

It's also a hint that there may be something wrong
with the model, such as the uniform prior on xsource
and ysource being too weak to keep the parameters away
from their boundaries if they're not supposed to be there.
(Or xsource and ysource being constrained --- why is
the source constrained constrained to fall on the grid
of observations?)

Are the log probabilities higher or lower for the
chain with pinned values?  And what happens to mu_raw?
A first step might be to look at the log probability
values for a sensible mu_raw over xsource and ysource
positions, or over several mu_raw values in a reasonable
range.  Just something like a gridded heat-map to get a sense
of modes in the posterior (if the posterior is truly
multimodal, sampling is problematic if the sampler doesn't move
freely between the modes).

Does the count data really look Poisson (i.e., does the mean
match the variance)?  Or is it more or less dispersed?

Initialization shouldn't be an issue because you'll
get initial values with medians xsource = ysource = 50,
i.e., in the middle of the constrained range.  And mu_raw
will get initialized with median value 1.  If these inits
aren't sensible, providing sensible initial values can
sometimes keep the chains from wandering off into regions
where they shouldn't.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I implemented a combination of the examples in the new version of the manual. I'm trying to perform joint hyperparameter fitting and predictive inference, by fitting over two feature dimensions to data (25 cases), and predicting the output of the GP for 200 test cases (predictive inference). The model compiles fine, but seems to be taking an incredibly long time to sample. I just cancelled the sampler, running in parallel on four cores, after about 5 hours (trying to take 1000 samples in four chains). Memory seemed to be fine.

Any suggestions for speeding this up? I'm not sure whether it makes sense to apply the Cholesky decomposition because Sigma is generated in the model block, so doing the Cholesky just adds more time each time (unless this is outweighed by the speedup of using multi_normal_cholesky?).

How will a model such as this scale with more data?

Note that I'm avoiding the analytical solution because I'm eventually moving to classification once I have this working satisfactorily.

Model and data file attached.

Best

Tom

messages.body_plain:
To answer the earlier question, it's still better to do the
Cholesky if you take more than one sample.  The multi-normal
does a Cholesky decomposition inside, so if there's only
one sample taken per covariance matrix, there's no difference.

I don't think the test case locations are going to cause
problems, but I don't have a lot of experience with GPs.
If you could test this and report back, it'd help all of
us -- just run a test with new points inside instead of outside
the range of the training points.

You can see if there are rejected samples by just measuring
how many times the parameter vector returned by NUTS changes from
iteration to iteration.  You can also look at the step size
and number of leapfrog steps (2^depth).  If the number of steps
is consistently large across chains, it's a strong hint that the
geometry of the posterior is complicated.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Here are some test results. I'm running these on a macbook pro 2.3 GHz i7 (each chain in parallel). To reiterate, this is a two-dimensional Gaussian Process model, predicting a test set from a training set, with hyperparameters on the covariance function as given for the Automatic Relevance Determination equation on page 80 of the manual. The first dimension of x is a constant (for testing purposes). I am running 4 chains for 200 iterations (100 warmup). Data were generated with a set seed in R, but the seed was free in Stan.

Run 1 (see test_data_1):

data:
25 training points, z-scored y values, 50 test points that span the range of the training set.

results:
time = 0.22 minutes.
stepsize in each chain (post warmup) = 0.356, 0.308, 0.303, 0.338
number of leapfrog steps (post warmup) = generally 8, a couple of 16s (2^3, 2^4).
number of rejections (post warmup) = 18, 5, 12, 13
(if I understood you correctly, I calculated the number of rejections by counting how many zeros there were in the diff of the unpermuted lp__ parameter in each chain).

Run 2 (see test_data_2):

data:
25 training points, unnormalised y values (range -62 -- 16), 50 test points that span the range of the training set.

results:
time = 0.48 minutes.
stepsize in each chain = 5.56, 6.11, 5.70, 5.68
number of leapfrog steps = generally 8, a couple of 16s (tree depths of 3 and 4).
number of rejections = 11, 22, 5, 7

Run 3 (see test_data_3):

data:
25 training points, normalised y values, 50 test points that are double the range of the training set (-2 to 2).

results:
time =  0.42 minutes.
stepsize in each chain = 0.28, 0.27, 0.37, 0.29
number of leapfrog steps = generally 16, a couple of 8s (tree depths of 3 and 4).
number of rejections = 9, 7, 35, 11

Run 4 (see test_data_4):

data:
25 training points, normalised y values, 100 test points that are double the range of the training set (-2 to 2).

results:
time =  2.00 minutes.
stepsize in each chain = 0.28, 0.26, 0.29, 0.32
number of leapfrog steps = generally 16, a few 8s and 32s.
number of rejections = 10, 7, 37, 20

So the main scaling factor seems to be the number of test points. The range of the test points doesn't seem to matter much. Not sure if this helps at all, and sorry if I've done something silly here.

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Sorry -- those have to be vectors the way multi_normal
is currently defined.

You can look in the index of the manual to see the
signatures for which each function is defined.
You'll see that multi_normal is only defined for
vectors, not row vectors.  So you can either
transpose (easy) or reorganize your data structures (more
efficient).

So

   row(y, i) ~ multi_normal(row(mu,i), Omega);

should transpose the rows into (column) vectors:

   row(y,i)' ~ multi_normal(row(mu,i)', Omega);

The more efficient approach would be to redefine
y to be an array of vectors, as in:

   vector[???] y[nData];
   vector[???] mu[nData];

   y[i] ~ multi_normal(mu[i], Omega);

The advantage of this latter approach is that once we've
vectorized the multi_normal, you'll be able to write it
all without the loop as:

   y ~ multi_normal(mu,Omega);

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Meaning of lp__ and model complexity
messages.body_plain:
lp__ is the total log probability accumulator.
What's required is that

    p(params|data) propto exp(lp__)

If you use plain old Stan, lp__ winds up being equal
to the joint log probability, log p(params,data), with
any term in the log probability that doesn't involve
a parameter dropped.

If you write your own models manipulating lp__ directly,
you just need to preserve the proportionality.  So
it might be log p(params|data) or log p(params,data).

- Bob
